utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Good morning, everybody. All the accused are present except accused Popovic, who sent a waiver. Prosecution is today represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Absent amongst the Defence teams, I notice Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon -- no, he is here. Sorry, I couldn't see. So not Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Lazarevic, and that's it. Good morning to you, Mr. Simic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to introduce a new member of our Defence team. It is Mr. Shah Noor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Shah Noor, you are most welcome, and good morning to you. So, Mr. Krgovic, you hadn't finished, I understand, yesterday. You still had a few questions to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had the whole night to ponder upon that, and after that I think that I will stick to my original time and that I will need another hour to finish. I've been sent a new list of documents -- or, rather, I sent you a new list of documents. I'll try and be as short as possible, but I think that I'll stick to my initial time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Simic, once again.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I showed you a document about the establishment of the army Republika Srpska. I need a clarification. This was the establishment of the army Republika Srpska, and at the beginning we saw the Main Staff with its sector, then corps with its units, and then at the end, independent units within the Main Staff. Would that be correct? My explanation of this document, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in your interview with the OTP in 2004, you spoke a lot about reporting and sending reports. The Prosecutor asked you how you sent reports to the Main Staff, and I wanted to remove an ambiguity that arose from that interview. Although in your examination-in-chief you already tackled that and explained to a large extent, but I want to concentrate on reports about morale. The reports that were sent to the superior command, irrespective of the area, were signed by yourself, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the documents that went from my commands were signed by me, and they were brought to me for signature by those who drafted it, and that included my assistant for morale who dealt with his part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you sent your regular combat reports, the part of -- about morale, was part of that combat report together with other parts dealing with other topics?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, when you sent interim report on morale in your unit, those reports were sent by you, and you sent it directly to the commander along the line of the subordination and in keeping with the principle of the unity command, which was in place in the army of Republika Srpska; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's correct, and that's how documents were received. They all arrived at my desk, and then I distributed the documents among the organs. What dealt with combat morale would be forwarded to my assistant for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that should have been the working principle in the army Republika Srpska, and you went -- you adhered to that when you joined the General Staff of the army Republika Srpska, so as you climbed up the ladder, you still continued to stick to the same principle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the way the army functioned. The military functioned in that way, and I adhered to that principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor in his interview put a lot of questions to you about the role of morale, the importance of morale for the army Republika Srpska, and you provided quite a lot of details in answering to the Prosecutor's question -- questions about morale. In answering the Prosecutor's questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friends, this is page 171 of the witness interview that was provided in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You provided a lot of details. I will not read the entire portion; correct me if I'm wrong in paraphrasing that part. Within the system of the military, morale is second in significance immediately after the training of the commands and units; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you assess the combat readiness of a unit, that combat readiness is assessed according to a set of elements. The first element is the command or the system of command and communications. That's the first element. The second element is the unit's morale. The third element is education and training. After that, follow logistics and all the other things. Your Honours, the tradition of our army, of our military, is to consider that if a fighter is ready to sacrifice his life for the interests and goals of a war, then he will do it even when undersupplied and when he misses some other elements necessary for warfare. I am not underestimating other elements that do have an impact on the combat readiness of a unit, but the notion of morale in a war that we waged, when the state of war was never declared, and when the entire structure of one's society underwent a major change, because we left the socialist system and went straight into a war, and in the meantime, there was no new system put in place to replace the old system. The elements that served as the foundation of morale until then all of a sudden became marginal, negligible, amongst other things, socialist, self-management, morale, [indistinguishable], the legacy of the national liberation war, the fraternity and unity that we had before the war; and all of a sudden we lost all that, and we had to find some new foundations to base combat morale on. There was one element, of course, and that was a general threat for the people, but we had to go back to our traditions from the times when kings ruled, and we had to go back to our religion. That's what we had to resort to. All those things compounded the situation when we had to prepare units and individuals for combat and when we had to assess their morale on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, there are several factors that impact morale, as you've just told us. In addition to the military elements, to call it that way, there are other elements, for example, the way a soldier is armed; wouldn't that be correct? I see a nodding, which means that you have answered positively to my question. Secondly, how he is trained, clothed, fed, how his family is taken care of, so all these factors come into play, and they practically involve all the organs of a command. And the underlying goal is to achieve this objective, to have a soldier well-prepared to fight?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, everything's correct, but primarily it is the situation in a society, the functioning of authorities. This is something that has a major impact on morale. The assistants for morale cannot create morale. Morale is created by an entire society, by the whole of a military organisation, and the Supreme Commander is primarily responsible for morale and then all the commanders below him; and assistants for morale are just professional organs who monitor the state of morale and propose or suggest things to the commander based on their estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have just prompted me to put my next question. You are talking about the significance and importance of morale, but not of the significance and importance of the organ of morale. When you emphasize his role on a large scale of the factors that impact combat readiness, you are talking about morale but not the importance of the assistant for morale?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the commander is responsible for the situation in his unit across all elements. In order for him to be able to incorporate that into his command function, he has assistants for each of these elements. How important is an element at a given situation depends largely on the situation. For example, when we have problems with the ammunition, fuel, or the state of replenishment of our unit, then the most important person would be the assistant for logistics. And when the internal organisation is at risk, then it is the assistant for intelligence who is most important. If we want to weigh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but as far as I know the witness did not -- didn't say the word "if." It is page 6, line 14. It was without word "if." I didn't hear the word "if."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I mean, just next time wait until he finishes what he is saying, and then we can correct it at the end of his statement. This way, we have interrupted him halfway through answering a question unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic. Sorry for the interruption. I had stopped you at the following: "And when the internal organisation is at risk, then it is the assistant for intelligence who is most important. If we want to weigh ..." That's where you stopped. If you could continue from there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The essence of the matter lies in the fact that you can't really weigh exactly the prevalent importance of an element in a given situation. In the hierarchy functions, it all depended on the rank of the assistant. That was one of the factors. If that person had a higher rank and more experience, he would be the most important among my assistants. Colonel Jelacic was my assistant for morale, and I was fortunate in having him because he had a lot of experience. He was very important to me as a person, as a colleague, as my second in command, not only when it came to the assessment of morale, but that is my specific trait. I don't want to have this spilling over to the Main Staff or some other commands. That was me, and that was my command. I am not saying that it applied across the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Unlike you who respected your assistant for morale, before with this Trial Chamber we heard the testimonies of commanders of certain units who believed that morale primarily depended on the commander and not on somebody who is sitting in an office sending him studies on morale, which very often have nothing to do with what is happening in the field. Are you aware of such attitudes towards assistants for morale in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also said that the commander was the person the most important for morale, and I -- I believe that this is the most important and the basic thing, but I am also saying that the position of the assistant for morale is also very important when the commander needs assistance and help in his function, and his function is command and control. There were cases when the role of the assistant for morale was minimized, but I believe that the commanders who thought that way did themselves this service because they complicated things for themselves unnecessarily. Their system of decision-making and command of their unit suffered as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the Prosecutor next asked you whether the army of Republika Srpska or the commander of the army Republika Srpska could command the military without the organ for morale, and you said: "No." I would kindly ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I believe we have a problem with translation. I am going to read in English, because my learned friend has just suggested that what has been transcribed does not correspond what was said during the interview. [In English] "Could Mladic have run the VRS without a morale department at the Main Staff?" You say -- your answer was: "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, I've shown you the establishment of the army Republika Srpska. That's what you saw yesterday. If we were to adhere to the rules, could Mladic have led the military without any one of the organs that are envisaged by the establishment? I'm talking about finance, logistics, morale, personnel, all the organs that are envisaged by the establishment. The way I understood your answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want my colleague to clarify wherever he is talking about the staff organs or the unit organs, the unit command organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecutor's question in the interview was also ambiguous. When he says "Main Staff" in his question, by the same token when I am talking about this, I'm talking about the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, could you kindly read the question in English, again? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "Could Mladic have run the VRS without..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without a morale department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "... a morale department at the Main Staff?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We've had a minor issue with the transcript, but I believe that now you understand my question. The way I understood your answer, because before that you spoke about the establishment of the military, the Main Staff, and your unit, and then the next question was put to you specifically about the organ for morale, not about any other organs, and in that way you were led, in my view, to raise the significance and importance of the role of the organ for morale in the Main Staff. I'm asking you, given the establishment and the way you answered the previous question, would you say that this applies across the board to all the organs of the Main Staff? Would I be right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, every organ has its own place. If we could do without any one of them, they would not have been incorporated into the establishment; hence, if Mladic could have done without his organ for morale, he would have eliminated his organ for morale and he would have sent his men in to fight without him. The essence of the matter is this: Not only could he not do without his organ for morale, he could not do without anybody, but the problem is how much he was willing to accept his organ for morale's proposals. But at the end of the day, the commander is the one who is in charge of decisions, and if he did not listen to his -- the suggestions of his assistant for morale, the mistake is his if the situation turns against him. But that's the commander's risk, a risk that he has to take. A wise commander will listen to his associates, to his assistants, because we in the military say, the more heads, the more they know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- well, as far as I understood your response, Witness, it's up to the commander what weight he will give to each particular organ in any specific situation or in general?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've said previously, depending on the situation, a particular organ can be engaged to a greater or lesser extent; and the commander is the one who decides. I think I've been quite clear on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, after this interview, you gave another interview to the Prosecutor in 2007; and answering the Prosecutor's questions - and this is on page 83 - speaking about General Gvero, you said the following: "Gvero was not allowed to issue orders either. He was perhaps the fifth on the list who are allowed to say something. Whatever you have for Gvero, anything, to accuse him of anything is ridiculous. During half the war, Mladic and Gvero were not on good terms. They were in an argument with one another." Do you remember having said that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to prejudge your decisions here. This is my personal opinion concerning the guilt of General Gvero. What I said is correct, and I will confirm once again. They were on bad terms with one another, and General Gvero was handicapped in that he could not do his job properly. The proposals he gave to the commander, the commander didn't like. It would have been better for all of us if he had listened to him on many points. General Gvero, like all the commander's assistants and all the members of the staff, did not have the right to command except for the Chief of Staff of the General Staff, General Milovanovic, and the deputy of the commander of the Main Staff. That is the principle of unity of command which is respected and abided by in the army. General Gvero could issue orders only to his close associates in his own sector for morale, those five or six men around him. They were the only ones he could command and nobody else. And that was not actually command; it was control, because it was team work, and these were officers subordinate to him. Commanding implies issuing combat orders, issuing orders to the units, whereas control takes place within a certain organ or sector and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you had occasion to attend meetings of the extended collegium of the Main Staff where all the assistant commanders and corps commanders were present. Did it often happen that General Mladic failed to invite General Gvero to such a meeting and for you to meet his deputy or someone else from his organ at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the meetings in the Main Staff, I don't know what happened there; but at the briefings on combat readiness, regardless of the extent to which he respected General Gvero, Mladic had to invite him. He had to invite him because the rest of us would have asked why he wasn't there if he hadn't invited him. But I did hear that he was excluded for a time from decision-making --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, not decision-making, interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but from reporting, briefing, and making conclusions in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was General Gvero's relationship with the political leadership including President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming that you are in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I can add that if I could hear from the witness what his relation with General Gvero was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was supposed to be my last topic, but if you wish I can introduce it now with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's go in sequence. Let's go in order because, of course, His Honour is the senior person here, so his question comes first. I am aware, Your Honours, that General Gvero, as for many years, he had been a professor at the high political school of the JNA, the post-secondary school. He was felt to be someone from communist times because he had taught Marxism and philosophy, and they didn't like him. Quite openly, they didn't like him, and they gave him the nickname the Red Devil, alluding to his past as a professor and to the fact that he had been a member of the communist party. As for my relationship with him, General Gvero was the most senior person in the command, in the Main Staff, and also the oldest. He had been promoted to the rank of general far -- a long time before the rest of us had been promoted. We were young generals, and in the case of most of us, he had been our teacher in our post-graduate studies. In relation to the others, he was a humanist compared to all the others, both by his nature and by the nature of his job. Whenever there was a problem I had to solve, I first tried to go through him because I knew he would understand me. The problems I had with the Batkovic camp were connected with this. I hope I am not speaking at too great a length, but I just want to say that there I found about 90 civilians who were not supposed to be in a military camp under any heading. I ordered that these persons be released. We asked them where they wanted to go. They asked to go back to their homes, because someone from the local authorities had collected them from their homes, rounded them up, and put them in a military camp, and this was inappropriate because it was a prisoner of war camp and there were no grounds for these people to be there. I knew that the civilian authorities would attack me for this reason, and that's why I rang up General Gvero and told him what I had decided. I didn't ask for his approval. Had I asked for someone's approval, I would have called up General Mladic. He said to me, Be careful; make sure that some fools don't kill them; make sure they go over to the Muslim side across our demarcation line. I understood this to be his concern for the lives of these people. We asked again those unfortunate people, we asked them again where they wanted to go, but they insisted that they wanted to go back to their homes, so we sent them back to their homes. It's true that I was attacked by the top-level authorities for this reason, but General Gvero protected me in the Main Staff, and so I did not have to suffer any consequences, and I think we did a good job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you for your exhaustive reply and explanation. I will now move on to another topic. In his interview from 2004, the Prosecutor put some questions to you and showed you a number of documents. I will now show you one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document P33, please. Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, you are going to skip the issues of Mr. Gvero's relation with Karadzic? This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because I have a specific topic. I will keep that for my last portion of the -- I would like to show him some documents and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I was just to remind you of the topic you had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This topic is directly connected to the relation between General Simic and General Gvero, which is why I want to deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you remember being shown this document by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, Your Honours. He asked me how come General Gvero was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he suggested several answers to you. He asked you whether General Gvero -- let me just for the sake of the transcript, let me say that this is on page 89 of the interview of 2004. The Prosecutor asked you whether Gvero issued commands to the forces, and your answer was no. He asked you further, if Mladic wanted to reach Krstic, did he go through Gvero at the forward command post; your answer was no. And then you spoke in general terms about the situation that occurs when a commander goes out into the field and he takes his team with him. You said, I assume when General Mladic went to visit a unit he always put together a team to accompany him, so I assume, as he was the assistant for morale and worked international organisations, that that was the reason he took him with him. And then you put forward another assumption, towards the end of this topic; it's also clear what Krstic said to Mladic about what was happening. He could have or was able to check this with Gvero who was independent there. And then the Prosecutor suggested a further question: This team put together by Mladic to observe these operations which were taking place, that was that was the reason why Gvero was at the forward command post. And you say, after the Prosecutor's question, formulated in this manner, "I think that's how it was. There could have been another reason, but under normal circumstances that would be the case." The Prosecutor suggested a possibility to you here. You said: "I assume ..." I'm telling you now that there is another possibility, that Gvero - and witnesses have testified to this - was on his way to Belgrade and dropped in at the forward command post, called up the Main Staff to he tell them he was there, and then continued on his way. Do you allow for this possibility, also, and did it happen that when Gvero was travelling towards the west, he would drop in to see you either at the forward command post or at the command, and what would happen on those occasions? Could you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the beginning of my testimony I said that I did not know and was not aware of how the operation in Srebrenica unfolded because I was not involved in it or informed about it. The questions put to me by the Prosecutor were questions I answered in general terms, about what would happen as a rule without actually knowing what had happened in that specific instance, and that's why you should take my response with reservations. If a forward command post is established, that's what happens. That's what I was saying. Some years later, I learned that a forward command post had not been established, that Mladic had not brought a team with him, and that Gvero chanced to pass that way and the road was blocked, and then he dropped in at Vlasenica to see what was going on. I was not categorical in my reply, and I said so in the interview. I do not wish to accuse General Gvero. He could not have issued command to Krstic if he was there because Mladic was with Krstic. He was not authorised to issue commands, and he was not authorised to monitor Krstic, either. He probably just dropped in and then was given a task as he happened to be there, but his job was to deal with journalists and with international organisations for the most part. I hope I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, did it happen sometimes that General Gvero would drop in to see you either at your forward command post or the command of your corps when he was passing by unannounced?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike General Miletic, who rarely left the Main Staff because of the nature of his job, the other assistants of the commander of the Main Staff would frequently visit the units; and whenever they were on their way towards Banja Luka - that is, towards the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps - they would always drop by to see me, find out what was going on, refuel their vehicles, and so on, and I was always pleased to see them. They were all my colleagues and friends. I tried to be a good host. General Gvero was a passionate smoker, and he would always be very pleased if I set aside some cigarettes for him because I was a non-smoker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when General Gvero came to see you in your unit, he would call up the staff to tell them he was with you so that if there was anything to be passed on or conveyed, that could be done. I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am waiting for the interpretation to finish. Your Honours, that is correct. That's correct because the trip would take several hours sometimes, so he would make a call to see if there was anything new, if there were any new tasks for him and so on, and then he would continue on his way on his original task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I wanted to show a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, if you are moving away from this document, while we have this document in front of us: General Simic, I understand your explanation that General Gvero was not in the position to issue any command or order, et cetera. But I wonder whether you could tell us why General Tolimir inserted, added General Gvero as one of the recipient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he's here informing General Gvero about the order of the Supreme Commander, because, probably, there was to be a press conference or something of that sort so that he would be informed. It's not an order. This is information, information he probably needed in order to carry out his main task, his job, especially as relations with UNPROFOR are mentioned here, and that was his constant duty, to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 6D137, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I assume you haven't seen this document before. It's a document sent by President Karadzic to General Gvero. Does this document and the tone of the document reflect the relationship between General Gvero and President Karadzic in the course of the war? The document is dated 1994, and it dates from December of that year.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first, it's inappropriate for the Supreme Commander to communicate directly with the assistant commander of the Main Staff. If he had any comments or objections, this should have been sent through the commander of the Main Staff. Secondly, the tone here is political. That's not how you talk to a soldier. And in the last sentence, military language is used. This was some sort of a fierce argument, and one can see that the Supreme Commander was very intolerant towards General Gvero and really didn't like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, is it -- do you know that in April 1995 at an assembly of Republika Srpska a decision was made for General Gvero to be pensioned off and replaced and that this was done at the initiative of President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, throughout the war there were attempts to replace not only General Gvero as the assistant for morale in the Main Staff but also the assistants in the brigades to be replaced by persons from the SDS party. We opposed this because those persons, apart from their party commitments, had no other qualifications to carry out those tasks and those jobs; specifically, the initiative to replace him came from several deputies, and evidently it was supported by President Karadzic. And regardless of the fact that in a certain period General Mladic was not on good terms with General Gvero, he opposed this decision and refused to replace his assistant. I don't know whether this was an expression of solidarity with Gvero or General Mladic's intolerance and dislike of the Supreme Commander, or - and this would be more understandable for me - because Gvero was an expert for his job and there was no one else who could replace him there. Maybe that was the reason for this decision. But, Your Honours, these are all my own thoughts. I have no specific evidence to support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Miroslav Deronjic was supposed to take the position of the assistant for morale in the Main Staff, thus replacing General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is just another proof how politicians thought. That person did not have any qualities that would qualify him for that position. This gentleman was nothing but a member, albeit highly positioned members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your interview on page 215 - I am talking about the interview that you provided in 2004 - you used the term describing yourself, i.e., you used a sentence to describe yourself. And you said that the worst thing in the world for a person to be is an unwanted child or an unwanted [as interpreted] general. This is what you said when you referred to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to correct something in the transcript. Unloved General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a bit farfetched, Your Honours. However, the authorities used us as professionals; still, they never trusted us and never liked us. One thing about that animosity was the fact that General Gvero was before all of us; he was the least loved or the most hated of all of us, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But General Mladic also did not care too much about you, as far as I could tell from this interview.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would not go into there. General Mladic had his own moments. He went through different periods, and I always spoke my mind. And when the indictment was issued against him, I told him that he should withdraw. He refused that, and he saw that as treason, as my personal offence of him. But I was only being honest and sincere. I spoke my mind. I told him what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you for your answers. I am now moving very briefly to another topic, which concerns the developments in March 1995. In the course of your testimony, you have spoken about the Muslim offensive on Mount Majevica, as a result of which you lost some positions, and you lost some territories, and the transformer in Stolice came under threat. That was in March, was it not? Correct me if I'm wrong. Looking at the combat reports that were shown to you, I could tell that Spreca and everything surrounding that operation was taking place in March 1995. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's precisely the period when all the things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You had quite a busy schedule in those days, and you had a lot of problems in your unit. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Majevica all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in answering Miletic's Defence questions, you were speaking in very general terms about the drafting of directives issued by any body, the Supreme Command, the Main Staff, in very general terms. Let me ask you very concretely: In March 1995, did you receive from the Supreme Command a request to submit your thesis for a directive that was in the pipeline?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when a directive is being prepared, one of the ways to contribute and submit materials is to analyse combat readiness. It can be done in a more direct way by asking from operative forces to submit a detailed report on certain issues, which then allows the Supreme Command to carry out proper planning. There are several occasions when we are asked to do that by the Main Staff and by the Supreme Command. I believe that the Supreme Command did ask us to answer certain questions for this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I can remember, you did answer their request?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, but it was inappropriate for the request to reach commands directly. It didn't go through the Main Staff. And then, following the proper procedure, we sent our answer to the Main Staff, which then forwarded it to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Krgovic. It's all right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 6D311. Can the witness please be shown the second page of the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be the second page in English as well. We are interested in the signature. Can we now go back to the first page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a stamp of your command, but this is not your signature. I can see here "za," on behalf of, and somebody's signature. Who signed the document on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that I had been on Majevica on that time. We processed this document, we analysed the document, at our joint meeting. We agreed that it should be typed up, and I authorised the duty operations officer at the time, Colonel Gengo, to sign on my behalf and to dispatch it, because when the document was ready for dispatch I was no longer at the command. In order to avoid any delays in the dispatching of the document, I authorised him to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: These are a thesis for Directive Number 7, aren't these?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it arises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't get what you said, and I don't think the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date on the document is 24th of March. The General has just told us that they discussed the document earlier and that he authorised his chief of operations and training to draft the document and dispatch it because he, himself, was on Mount Majevica at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that he was the duty operations officer. It so happened that he was also the chief of the operations and training. He is -- he was the one who drafted the document. The document was first produced in a handwritten form, and then it was verbatim typed up. I initialed it in the handwritten form, and I authorised the duty operations officer to send it on my behalf. He was at the command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction for the transcript. Just a correction in the transcript. One witness's "yes" was not recorded. The witness said "yes" to my question, whether these were the thesis for Directive Number 7, but that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you answered "yes" to this question, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did answer yes, but, again, the answer has not been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you speak up and say "yes"?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after so many years and so many dates, I can't be a hundred per cent sure of the date, but it would be roughly around that time, and I believe that one can establish a link between the date and the development in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, it transpires from the document that it was sent to Major General Subotic, the advisor to the president, and he was the same person from whom you had received a request to provide your input for the directive. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says in the document that the document answers to the advisor's question. However, the document with the accompanying letter was sent to the General Staff because it was not appropriate for me to communicate directly with the advisor of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Among the various inputs in the document, nothing was taken into account as far as I could tell, and this was clearly your position that you had put forward in some earlier occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask the witness to remove the headsets to avoid all confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. He understands English, too, so I think he will have to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But she's speaking in French but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but -- she's speaking in French. It will be translated into English, and someone has to reply in English. So let's see what your question is or what your comment is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the speculations of my colleague are going much too far, because to say that in the directive these proposals were not accepted, okay. But here we see the date, 24th of March; the directive is dated 8th of March, so perhaps we need to establish first of all if the proposals were drawn up for Directive Number 7 or for something else, and I would like to ask my learned colleague to indicate the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think insofar -- I don't know, my colleagues would or would not agree with me. If they don't, please speak up. But insofar as he's giving this Directive 7 an interpretation of his own, he's got a right to give it an interpretation of his own and ask questions. With regard to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you can deal with it on redirect in any case. As regards the source of the document, perhaps Mr. Krgovic can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, General, please put your headphones back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is there any doubt in your mind that this document maybe does not originate from your corps, that it maybe was not drafted in your command?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking at the heading. This is the letterhead of my corps. The document was filed on the last page. I can see the signature of the person whom I authorised to sign it, and it also bears a stamp of my corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The contents of the document corresponds to what you had discussed at the command meeting and what you drafted in handwriting, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you then allow me, please, to read the entire document to be absolutely certain? A lot of time has passed, and I can't be entirely sure what I am being asked about. Can I be given some time to read the entire report, and then I will be able to answer with a higher degree of certainty. Maybe something has been changed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Both of you. Would 20 minutes be enough for you, 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need five. I am a fast reader, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we are going to give you 20 because we are going to have the break now as we announced yesterday. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question on the source, the source from which my colleague obtained this document, that's what I am interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we'll deal with all this -- 20 minute break, and we'll deal with all this when we reconvene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's continue. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, were you able to look at this document? To the best of your recollection, the contents of this document correspond to what you discussed at your command and what you ordered to be done, letters in compliance with a request from the Supreme Command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not a request for a directive. This is a completely different document which stemmed from the serious situation on the western front where at the request of General Milovanovic a state of war was declared in two municipalities in the Krajina. And this gave him much more favorable conditions, and he was able to stop the advance and launch a counter-offensive, and to restore all the lost positions. In view of the fact that we had similar problems in our area, we also sent frequent requests, either that a state of war be declared or for some measures to be introduced, which would make it easier for us commanders to command. I wish to mention once again, Your Honours, that a war was being waged and the civilian authorities were living and working as if it was peacetime. They had office hours. They took annual leave. The coffee bars were full of men, especially in the wartime, and they -- there were not enough men at the front line. There was fuel for civilians at all the petrol stations. It could be bought for money, but there was no fuel for the army, and many other things were going on inappropriate to a country and a society which was in a state of war. A state of war, however, had not been declared, not to mention the fact that people were being killed and there was no state of war. So it would the appear that we were doing maneuvers and exercises. It was under these conditions that we asked for new conditions to be put in place because suddenly combat activities began on all the fronts because there was a major offensive on. We were asked to propose some of the measures that the civilians authorities were supposed to introduce because the thesis here are not military. These are things that we are proposing that the civilian authorities should do in order to assist us. Where I was, unfortunately, none of this was adopted by the civilian authorities. This document was not drawn up by the operations organ. It's just by chance that it was signed by Gengo because at the bottom on the left-hand side, you can see the initials of the person who drew up the document and the person who typed it out. The content of the document corresponds to the conclusion I arrived at based on consultations with my associates. Your Honours, I ask you not to doubt the reliability of this document because it was signed on my behalf by Gengo. He was an associate I trusted implicitly. Had I not trusted him, I would have replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of Their Honours - and Mr. Simic, I have the original of this document - if there are any doubts about its reliability, if any party wishes to inspect the document I have it available. Mr. Simic, I agree with you when you say that when the Supreme Command, which incorporated both the military and civilian authorities, asked you for proposals as to how certain political issues should be resolved and that an overall political strategy be adopted, which is how I understood your document; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope I was clear. The terminology is not military. These are political issues and are proposals as to what the civilians authorities should do to improve the conditions in the army for the implementation of its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what you wrote in this document is what you said at the briefing on combat readiness in January of that year as you testified a few days ago before this Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these problems had persisted since the beginning of the war. The war was in its fourth year and I think had been resolved, and even after this, nothing was resolved, because there was no political will for the war to end in peace and without undue delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it's logical that when the president of the republic wants to set up a political framework for the directive and to have consultations and draw up the thesis for the directive, that he should ask for suggestions and collect information and proposals from various organs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the president probably consults his political organs concerning political issues. It was surprising to us that the army was asked to give proposals concerning political issues. Nothing had been done previously, none of this, and we except this to yield some results, but unfortunately it didn't. He sought our opinion here, and he did not take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's normal when the president is drawing up a directive to ask for the opinion of the Ministry of Defence when he's assessing the security situation or the security situation that he should ask for the opinion of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, and so on and so forth when drawing up some non-military parts of the directive; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understand this document. Your Honours, I have never been a president, but common sense tells me that that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in March 1995, the only directive that was drawn up was Directive Number 7; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether any other directive was drawn up, but this one, the number 7, is the only one that reached us, and it was followed by specific orders. Later, there was another one which was drawn in the Krajina over there and had to do with the fall of municipalities in western Krajina, but that directive unfortunately arrived with a delay and could not be implemented because of the conditions in the war theater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As there are certain discrepancies in the date and as you, as you said, were facing a very difficult situation at Majevica, this does not mean that it relates to another request. Did you get any other request from the Supreme Command apart from this one which you responded to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness clearly indicates on page 29 -- 28, line 9, that this request concerning this document is not a request for the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, but the witness said to the military part of the directive. Now he's talking about the political framework of the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. Let him answer the question. I think -- you have a very valid point, Ms. Fauveau. I'm not arguing the point raised, but I think we have got a very straightforward, intelligent witness here, and he can give us a straight answer. Thank you. I know I have made you happy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This has made me happy, indeed. Let me say again, the directive had already been drawn up, but the same requests happened to be in the directive because we had been repeating them like parrots for years. This is another document which arrived after the directive. It did not come from the Main Staff but from the advisor to the former minister, General Subotic, and it was sent directly to us, bypassing the General Staff, which was inappropriate. And in a way, it was actually politics interfering in command, because any bypassing of authority is highly detrimental to the army. I don't know what specifically the Defence counsel is getting at, because one in the same question is constantly repeated, but I think this has nothing to do with Directive Number 7. It does have to do with the emergency measures which the president -- the Supreme Commander introduced in certain municipalities in the Krajina, and our request that the same be done in our territories where there was intensive combat going on to make our life easier. I am available to clarify if anything needs clarification, but I continue to assert that this is not linked to the directive. It's only by chance that the same points are raised, because we had written three or four such requests previously to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I accept what you say. It's your opinion. The document speaks for itself. It says here that these are thesis proposed, so I don't want to enter into a polemic with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, one moment. Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, if Mr. Krgovic reads the part that makes up the body, it says here "proposals" -- let me read to the end. "Proposals for the directive to the RS President on special measures in the IBK zone of responsibility." Please, these are extraordinary measures. This is not a regular directive. Let's not keep going back to the directive when the directive has no connection with this document. I don't know what is supposed to be achieved here. We keep running around in circles. I thought this was going to be over two hours ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me explain something to you, General. Mr. Krgovic, who is representing General Gvero here, has a right -- he's cross-examining you, and as such he's got a right to put questions. He may at times be in agreement with what you say, sometimes in disagreement with what you say. You may hold different opinions. But he has a right to ask you further questions to make sure, if there is something he doesn't agree with in your testimony, that he obtains more clarification from you. So I am going to suggest to Mr. Krgovic, if he has further questions on this issue, to put them slowly. Try not to overlap, Mr. Krgovic, because you have been overlapping. And then, if you have further answers, you give them. If you have nothing to add to what you've stated earlier, leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while counsel are conferring, let me say that I have the best of intentions to assist, but as a person who has been efficient all his life, I try to make the best use of time and space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. No one doubts your intentions are to try and help us understand what really happened. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, when it says here "proposals for the directive," what directive is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says here -- let me repeat what it says here in the preamble: "The proposals for the directive of the president of Republika Srpska on special measures in the IBK zone of responsibility." So this refers to the directive of the Supreme Commander, that is, the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, another clarification about another topic, and I'll finish. When you described the conversation with General Gvero concerning Batkovic, in what year did that conversation take place? From your interview, I see it was 1992; is that correct? Is that the event you are referring to in your interview?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's correct. It was in 1992, either on the 5th or 6th of September, because I was taking up my duties, my new duties, and it was then that I learned about the situation in the Batkovic camp, which deeply disappointed me. I was a new commander there, and I had the best intentions of introducing order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Haynes, I understand you have a cross-examination, too, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Haynes starts, General Simic -- it's me here, not him. In answering Mr. Krgovic's question relating to Deronjic, you said that he was far from qualified; he's not qualified at all. But I don't think you actually answered the question whether or not you heard that Deronjic was supposed to be appointed as assistant for morale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not know who the person in question was at the time. I only learned subsequently. When this was happening, I didn't know who was being proposed, but I realised that it was somebody from the inner circle of the Serbian democratic party. And the intention, I suppose, was for the military to be politicised, and we in the military are strongly opposed to that attempt. As far as his personal skills are concerned, I don't know. The gentleman may have a university degree, but I had in mind the particular qualities that an assistant for morale, political and religious issues, have to have. You need special education for that. I hope that I've managed to clarify the matter for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, by any chance, who you heard that news or rumor from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even the Assembly talked about Gvero's replacement. It was no secret at all. It was, if anything, a public secret because it was aired on TV. It was just a matter of days when this would happen. At that moment, he was not in favour with anybody. The political authorities did not like him. His superior, General Mladic, was not particularly fond of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant Deronjic, not Gvero, not the replacement of Gvero, but specifically by Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't even know this man. The family name doesn't mean anything. He could have been called Simic for all I care. All I know is that he did not have the right qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have an estimate of how long you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So that means, Mr. Thayer, that you will start your cross-examination today. I don't suppose you will finish it today?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for clarification, we'll be breaking at noon as yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, General Simic. As you know, I represent Vinko Pandurevic who in 1995 was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. I want to start by asking you a number of questions which arise from the very long interviews you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor when I think it was anticipated you might be a Prosecution witness in the Perisic case; was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm going to try and take things chronologically as far as possible. Now, at the beginning of the war in Bosnia, when you arrived to the territory of Eastern Bosnia, there was a good deal of paramilitary activity in and around the town of Bijeljina, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I had quite a few problems before I was able to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've anticipated my next question. The paramilitary units in and around Eastern Bosnia didn't welcome the presence of army units, did they?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, paramilitaries are all those who don't want to be under the military command. When I came to the territory, I found several small groups, mostly from Serbia, with some self-proclaimed leaders who were engaged in operations independently on their own, but their most prevalent activity was plundering and other sorts of crime. My life was also at stake when I confronted them directly; my life came under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. You've answered my next question. In terms of the establishment of military units within the army of Republika Srpska, I want to address one particular problem, which I think you're aware of, and that was one of your subordinate commanders, the commander of the 3rd Samborski Brigade who was in fact murdered. Can you tell us what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I found a certain number of units there. On my personal initiative, we established two more brigades and we reorganised another one. We -- or established a Majevica and a Siberia brigade, and I appointed two active servicemen as commander and Chief of Staff. They had been pensioned off, but then they were reactivated upon my proposal. Unfortunately, when a shift was being sent to a position, a drunken soldier fired a burst of fire and killed both of them in the very centre of Bijeljina. Now, that soldier was subsequently tried, but this left a very somber impression on the entire military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever discover or establish any motive on the part of that soldier for the murder of his own commander?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the investigation established that the person in question had been drinking in town, had opened fire even before that and wounded a woman; and when the police came to arrest him, he offered resistance and he found shelter with a unit that was being assembled to go to the front line. He had already got on a bus when the police came and blocked the bus with an intention to arrest that person. The commander and the Chief of Staff got off, followed by several soldiers, and the drunken soldier wanted to deal with the police, and in trying to do so he killed his commander and Chief of Staff. I was not under any impression that it was premeditated, that it was his intention to kill them, that he had a motive of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I want to move on, please, to some comments that you've made in the past about General Mladic. Can we take it that during the four years of war you had a close working relationship with General Mladic and you knew him personally?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I would talk to him every day on the phone, and on several occasions he came to my unit; he inspected my subordinated units together with me, and we also saw each other at briefings in the Main Staff. I kept my distance in this particular case because that was the way a soldier would behave. It was part of my military behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thus, it was your impression, wasn't it, that he was deeply affected by the death of his daughter and that that affected his style of leadership of the army?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Mladic had the misfortune of his daughter committing suicide, and I believe that he must have been deeply shaken as a human being, because for three months we could not communicate with him after that. I thought that when one suffered such a loss and such a shock, that such a person should not perform any responsible tasks for a while. This should have been done because he suffered high intensity stress, and in my personal view under such circumstances no man could be expected to show normal reactions and normal judgments. On the other hand, he himself as a person was quite independent, and it may not be my call to say so, but he was also very stubborn, and very often he would not take anybody's proposal into account, and he was very independent. He had his own will when he made decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The three adjectives I drew from your earlier interview, and I was going to ask you if you still agreed with, was that he became more difficult to deal with, vengeful, and dictatorial. Would you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And before the General answers, Mr. President, if we could have just some time-frame that we are talking about. That might make the testimony a little bit more helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Can you help us as to when General Mladic's daughter died? And I'm sure it's a matter we can agree between us and the Prosecution so that we have got a time-frame, can't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's cut it short. If you know the date, please, we don't need the witness to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the precise date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it happened in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Going back to the original question, did you find him to be vengeful, more dictatorial, and more difficult to deal with?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the fact is that he was no longer the same person. This certainly left a mark on him. Whether he was more revengeful, in a certain way he was. He never spared himself, so he never spared us either. He was even more persistent, even more harsh, and he had even more demands upon us. However, due to the situation in the battlefield was such, we had millions of problems. When we thought that the war was nearly over, it only started then. I believe that another thing that had an impact on him were the convoys of refugees from Krajina whom he received in western Bosnia. Before the war, he served as a commander in the territory of Knin, and he was familiar with the region and with the people. It's very difficult for me, Your Honours, to talk about all this. He was no longer as cheerful as he was before, and that's a fact. Sometimes before that event, he would even joke with me; we would crack jokes. After this sad event, no such thing. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of his determination to have his own way, one of the things you said in your interviews on more than one occasion was that if somebody had stood up to him over the Srebrenica operation, they would have found themselves killed. Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a hypothetical question. I was not in Srebrenica. I don't know whether anybody stood up to him. It's all about the situation over there, and how could anybody have stood up to him? If his life was threatened, he would have reacted appropriately. When there was an attempt at my life -- actually, when there was that group that prepared to kill me, I had no choice but to arrest them. If somebody had opened fire, I would have killed them. If I were to say anything about his situation in Srebrenica and about his reaction to some hypothetical things, I don't think it would be appropriate for me to speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I have a slight suspicion that there may have been a mistranslation of your question. The way the witness answered your question makes me suspect that. Can you make a specific reference to any part of his interviews with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to leave the matter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to push it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on now, please, to more recent events. In the spring of 1995, as you've told us, you took place -- you took part in Operation Spreca. Now, that was an operation which involved not only the East Bosnia Corps but also units of the Drina Corps, specifically the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I hope I have understood what you have said about that operation correctly, that it was badly organised and chaotically coordinated between all the units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the operation was well-organised. However, the weather was bad; it was cold, and soldiers who mounted an attack and moved on for 2 kilometres, but then they did not have any way to find shelter. They had to return, so the result was zero. Second of all, the entire -- the Zvornik Brigade did not participate as a whole, and when two corps are involved or two brigades are involved, then if things don't go well, then one blames another. We saw the interview in which my colleague is blaming things on me, but the most important thing is that we did not achieve any successes, or if we did, our successes fell short of what we had planned. The operation was not badly planned; it was badly executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would I be right to suggest to you that during the whole of that operation, you did not speak to Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have noticed, but I've told you that the corps commander was present in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, so I did not talk to his subordinate but to the commander himself. I was at his operation post on the morning when the operation was launched, and I was there all day. In other words, I had my contacts and I talked to Mr. Pandurevic's superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But were you aware what combat activities the Zvornik Brigade were carrying out, and were they aware of what combat activities your units were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did know, Your Honours. We exchanged information. We occasionally met. The commander of the Main Staff was there, in my zone and in their zone. Let me clarify. I had received an order to organise our cooperation; however, the Zvornik Brigade was not subordinated to me. We worked together in cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. It may be that I have misunderstood you, but I had understood your evidence to be that the coordination of that operation was not good. Am I correct in that assumption or not?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a good plan for cooperation, but it was not acted upon. If one unit starts moving sooner than the other, then cooperation goes out of the window because cooperation is planned for a certain area and for a certain time; but if one unit does things at a different time and a different place, then there is no longer coordination or cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to leave the topic there, is that what happened in Operation Spreca 95?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what happened. The Zvornik Brigade was moving faster than my units. They wedged into the enemy's deployment lines, but then after a while, they had to withdraw to their initial positions. So at the end of the day, the operation was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave that, General Simic, and we're going to go to another topic, which is the ability of commanders to remove officers. And I'm going to show you the first document I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which is P702, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you stated the principle yesterday, but I think this is the document that provides the principle, which is that an officer of the rank of colonel and above can only be removed in effect by the president of Republika Srpska, can't he?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are very strict rules in the military as to who removes and appoints personnel. When I said that I removed my associate, I said that I did not personally remove him. I suspended him from his duties, and I requested from the Main Staff to remove him from his position because it was not I who had appointed him. If I did appoint anybody, it would be lower-ranking officers. So what I did, I could only do through the Main Staff. I could not remove anybody from their position because such an act had repercussions that are beyond my scope, the salary for the promotion and so on and so forth. What I could do was just to suspend a person. If he had been involved in crime, I could start criminal proceedings; if it was a matter of discipline, then there were disciplinary measures; and if I just did not like his style of work or if I did not cooperate well with him, I could send a proposal to my superior command to remove his from his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. But that sort of protection wasn't afforded to all ranks, was it? For example, as a brigade commander you could remove from office an officer of the rank of second lieutenant without seeking the approval of the Main Staff; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it depended on this person's position. If he was in a position acting as a captain first class or major, then the answer would be no because it would not have been within the brigade commander's purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, that's why I chose the rank that I did. A brigade commander could remove a second lieutenant, couldn't he, within this law?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, the answer is yes, but if that second lieutenant occupied a post that by establishment should be occupied by a person of his rank; however, if a second lieutenant occupied a post that called for a higher-ranking person, a captain first class or a major, then the answer is no. I thought I had made myself clear the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Simic, now you have. Thank you. I now understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 7D485 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in particular, General Simic, can you look at paragraph 3. Did you see this or a similar document to this in or about May of 1994?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
