utterances.text: Yes, I did, and this one is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we are clear, was this a restatement of a principle, or did this change the position vis-a-vis a commander's authority over his security organ?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my previous testimony I pointed out that assistants to the commander with respect to a certain element, such as the assistant for logistics, also follow the personnel situation - in this case, the logistical and rear personnel in the subordinate units - and draw up a chart, a working chart, and the organ for morale does the same. The same is done in the security area. The chief of the sector for security has to keep track on the security officers in the brigades and other units because these are persons who have to undergo special training, and they have to undergo a special check to make sure they're suitable for this service. No one can be appointed, no officer can be appointed, to a post without their approval. That's why I asked General Tolimir to replace my chief of security in the corps and give me somebody else. When I explained all this to the commander and to him, he took my opinion into account and sent me Lieutenant-Colonel Jakovljevic [as interpreted], who had been the security chief in the 30th Division in Banja Luka. He was an experienced security officer who adhered strictly to the rules. In this document, this officer is drawing attention to the fact that these people cannot be dismissed without approval because there were many attempts to downgrade these people, because if some civilians abused their positions and this is reflected in the army and an officer writes about this, then they say that the military is interfering, but it's all important for the military. And then they want to replace the security officer, and there is pressure from the civilian structures, just as they wanted to replace some morale officers, including General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for the intervention. At page 47, line 6, I believe the General named Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Todorovic, and it's just not captured, but just to avoid confusion later on, I think that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one more question on this document, General. In paragraph 3, the procedure for approval is outlined, and then somebody has underlined the words: "Not a single member of the VRS can be appointed or to dismissed from duties in security and intelligence organs of the VRS without this approval." Do you agree with that as a statement of the employment position of members of the security and intelligence organs?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my previous reply I said that these were persons who were especially trained for that duty. You can't take a battalion commander and appoint him chief of security unless he has gone through a course and been prepared because he will not be able to deal with a job properly, otherwise. And this is a warning to that effect, that persons should not be appointed according to someone's wishes, but that they have to be people who are qualified to perform this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to try one more time, General Simic; then I'm going to leave it. Is the underlined portion of that document correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Asked and answered twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Three times, and he just gave the answer "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed now. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to show you one further document, which is P2741.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can say it a fourth time if need be. I can say "yes" a fourth time if need be, so we don't have to return to the same question yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Don't worry, General Simic. We're not going to. We're going to move on to another one. I'm going to show you a another document, which is P2741.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, General Simic, can you have a look at it and see whether this a document that is familiar to you and a document that you saw in the latter part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know about this document. This is a warning, an instruction, as to how commanders should treat the specific organs, because evidently some of the them did not know how to behave towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you one very simple question. Did you take the view, when you first saw this document as a corps commander, that it changed the relationship between a commander and his security organ or merely restated the position as it was?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a trained officer, and I knew how one should treat the security organs. This is an instruction intended for those young commanders who had arrived without having completed any training beyond military academy, and they didn't know how to behave. So they made use of these people in ways other than what they were supposed to be doing. Nothing changed here. I acted like that even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will leave this topic now, General Simic. Now, I want to move on to something you were telling us about a unit from your corps that went to the Zvornik area. And just so we give it some background, your headquarters were in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that would be, would you agree with me, about a 120 kilometres from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about speaking to General Miletic on the telephone. Can you recall what date that was when you had the conversation with General Miletic on the telephone about picking up prisoners from the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not quite sure. I thought it was before the fall of Srebrenica, but following the trial of General Krstic, I thought that these prisoners would not be able to arrive in the primary school in Pilica before the fall of Srebrenica. So this was after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you recall whether it was at a time when, as you told us, you could hear artillery fire from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the fall of Srebrenica, artillery fire continued because the operation at Zepa was ongoing, and all this was across from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the month of July of 1995, did you only send the one unit to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't send a single unit to the Zvornik area. I -- in the border area between my corps and the Drina Corps, I sent a battalion commander of the military police with a military police company to the village of Pilica, to report there with the intention of taking prisoner a certain number of members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for exchange purposes. It was not our intention to participate in the combat activities. Actually, there were none in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it was a platoon. How many men was that, and whose command were they under?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said I didn't send the battalion commander to make the situation more serious because he was a major, whereas the battalion commander was a lieutenant, and there are 30 soldiers in a platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Platoon commander, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't send a platoon. I sent a company numbering about 80 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right, and how did they go to Pilica from Bijeljina? Presumably they were transported in some way?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ordered the commander apart from the establishment vehicles he has at his disposal to take a certain number of transport vehicles from his unit in order to be able to transport those soldiers when they were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it's about 30 men with a commander being transported and taking with them a number of transport vehicles; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood this correctly. I think there were two combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if we could have a look, then, please at the Zvornik brigade duty officers' notebook for the 16th of July of 1995. That's P377 at page 146, both in English and B/C/S. And we are looking for an entry at 1050.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see the entry at 1050 where it says: "35 soldiers from the Eastern Bosnia Corps were send to the forward command post"? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know where the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours. I didn't send anyone to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: These must be the soldiers that went -- that you thought had gone to Pilica, mustn't they? 16th of July, 35 soldiers from your corps being sent to the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade. This must be the unit that came from Bijeljina to Pilica as you believed.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this unit did not go further than Pilica. It didn't go beyond Pilica. Perhaps someone told him they would go to the forward command post, but they didn't. They didn't go beyond Pilica because in Pilica they came across a barricade, and the road was closed for traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: According to your recollection, how long was this unit of men out of your zone of responsibility and in Pilica? When did they come back?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, like every normal commander, I expected our opponents to launch an assault on the forces -- on our forces to cut off the corridor and draw out our forces. Under normal circumstances, that would have been what was expected, so I took my forces and went to the corridor. I was there in the area of Brcko, and I came back at around 1800 hours, and I met the battalion commander while driving through the town. He was wearing a civilian suit. He was wearing civilian clothes. I stopped and I was angry. I said, Why are you not performing your task? And he said, We came back right away. And I said, Why did you come back? Why didn't you carry out the task? And he said, When we got to Pilica, in the school we found people there. They gave them to us. We transported them. There they are in Batkovic. They're having lunch, they're having a bath, and they're being listed by the Red Cross. I was a bit angry, and then I had to apologise for thinking that he hadn't completed the task. This unit did not go beyond Pilica, and it came back very quickly. It did not participate as a combat unit but more as an escort unit transporting prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I wonder, therefore, in the light of that answer whether we can look at page 185 of the zone duty officers' notebook, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what you need to focus on, General Simic, is the bracketed section right in the middle of the page where it says: "Deputy commander called from Bijeljina, the unit from Baljkovica is to be sent back to Bijeljina..." and the platoon was sent to Bijeljina. Now, this is the Zvornik Brigade duty operations officers' logbook for the 26th of July. Did you have any knowledge as commander that a platoon of your men were in the Baljkovica forward command post area of the Zvornik Brigade for ten days?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now -- first, we're talking about the police, and now we're talking about a platoon from Baljkovica. Baljkovica is not in my area. It's in the border area between the East Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps. I don't know what a platoon in Baljkovica would be doing going to Bijeljina, if it was from Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can we have a look at P3 for a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished, please. I haven't finished. Your Honours, not a single unit of the East Bosnia Corps participated in the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I just want to see if I can help you with what this entry means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're going to have a look at P346, which is the regular combat report for the 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you look at the last bullet point under paragraph 2, because this clears up any ambiguity in the duty officers' logbook, where it says: "At its own request, the police platoon from Bijeljina was sent back to its destination." So it wasn't a unit from Baljkovica. That's where it was being deployed. It was a unit from Bijeljina, which must make it the same police unit you've been talking about, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, in the second part we can see that there was an ambush in the areas of Pantorica [phoen], Rabic, and the school in Baljkovica, which means that Baljkovica is in the area of the Drina Corps. Secondly, the police platoon from Bijeljina doesn't have to be a military police platoon from Bijeljina. It's the civilian police, not the military police. So please don't mix up the civilian police and the military police. The civilian police came to Pilica [as interpreted], took these prisoners, took them to Batkovic, and came back in a matter of three hours, and they had nothing to do with the combat operations in the area of the Zvornik Brigade. That's an insinuation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I just want to show you one more document before we finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's 7D712, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, especially right at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a clarification for the transcript. The transcript says: "The civilian police came to Pilica..." and I'll just leave it there. I just want to note that in case it needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. I hadn't spotted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to tidy that up because I just want to show this gentleman one more document, and then I'll finish at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient to you, we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course, the prison camp at Batkovici was within your, as it were, zone as commander of the East Bosnia Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were just telling us about how the commander of this police platoon had told you later the same day that the people he had collected had been registered by the Red Cross and were sitting having a meal or something; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could have a look. It's just perhaps the second page of this document, so that the witness can see the substance of it rather than the cover. There should be a list of names, so can we try the third page. Thank you. Can we turn that around so that the witness can identify what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a document like that before, General Simic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I did not deal with exchanges. There was a commission that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But were you aware that -- that prisoners taken to Batkovici were registered and this sort of information was taken from them?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the normal procedure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'll have to leave it there. But just one last thing. In relation to this excursion by a police platoon to Pilica, who did you inform that they were coming in the Zvornik Brigade or the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said three times that I asked General Miletic to contact them and tell them that this unit be arriving. He promised me he would do that and that I could begin preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you check back with him whether he had and who he had spoken to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed this on to the duty operations officer because I -- as I told you, I had to go to the Brcko corridor urgently, so I didn't check that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the duty operations officer of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We met briefly in the witness room a couple of days ago, but allow me to introduce myself formally for the record. My name is Nelson Thayer. I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, sir, during your service as a JNA officer, is it fair to say that except for the three years - I believe you spoke about - in Sarajevo at the Viktor Bubanja barracks, you sent most of your career at the 329th Armoured Brigade at the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I also spent two stints in education in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I'd like to do, General, just briefly, is get a better idea of the geographic territory covered by your corps' area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2108. That's also map 3 in the map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of quick questions just to give us a better idea of the lay of the land in your territory. Sir, we can see, at least in English, the East Bosnian Corps in the upper right-hand corner of the map with Bijeljina marked there. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I can see that. However, the map does not reflect the true situation, because the corps went westwards up to the river Bosna, whereas here I can see the area depicted only up to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And we have the Drina river to your right border and the river Sava to the north; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And then from the mouth of the river Bosna to the town of Modrica, and then it follows the ethnic border all the way to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just mentioned Brcko. In addition, you also had the Ugljevik obstina in your AOR; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for your information, in my AOR there were the following municipalities: Bijeljina, Ugljevik, Lopare, Brcko, Pelagicevo, Samac, and a part of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as we can see from the map, your corps was contiguous to the south with the northern-most reach of the Drina Corps and the Zvornik municipality, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with the map. Let me move along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to identify some of your key staff in 1995. We've heard some names, and we've seen some names in documents, and we may see a few, so let me just make sure I've got some of these members of your command and staff correct. In 1995, was Colonel, later Major-General, Budimir Gavric your Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was Colonel Radenko Gengo still your ops chief in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radenko Gengo was not my ops chief. He was the assistant Chief of Staff, Budimir Gavric, for operations and training. Your Honours, I would kindly ask you to take into account that the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska was taken over from the establishment of the former JNA, which was based on the Russian doctrine and the old kingdom of Yugoslavia's doctrine. The Prosecutor mentions this ops chief, which is part of the NATO structure and plays a different role than our chief of operations and training. In NATO, the assistant for operations is in command of operation. He has the right to command. Our assistant for operations and training does not have the right of command, either at the level of the brigade or the corps level or the Main Staff level. Please make sure you take this into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And was the late Colonel Slobodan Jelacic still your assistant commander for morale in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, in 1995 was Colonel Milenko Todorovic still your security chief?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Todorovic, colonel, was the security chief in my corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was he the security chief who replaced the one you spoke about yesterday, or was there one in between?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must go back a bit further. Milenko Todorovic was initially there for three months, and then for family reasons - he had some problems - he had to leave Bijeljina, and he was replaced by his deputy, a young major who had a rather hard time finding his ground. And then he was replaced by Colonel Petar Jakovljevic at my request. Unfortunately, he has died in the meantime. Before that, he was the chief of security in the 30th Infantry Division of the 1st Krajina Corps. After a year, maybe a year and a half, he returned to the 1st Corps, and Todorovic returned to his original position where he remained until the end of the war. So this would be my correction of that part of the interview from which I omitted this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Now, in the AOR of your corps, there was a Main Staff logistics base, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. According to our rules, in the zone of responsibility you can also find a unit that is directly tied to the Main Staff. In my case, it was the 35th logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was located in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was headquartered in the Vojvoda Stepa barracks in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we were to see that abbreviated, it would be written 35 POB; do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be 35.Pob. Its commander was Colonel Jovo Kundacina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This may be an obvious question to you, General, but that means it wasn't under your direct command, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Although it was in my zone, it was not under my command. However, due to some problems in the garrison, we had to cooperate. In addition to that, I also had a Prosecutor's Office and a corps, which were also not under my command. But I had to provide them with my military policeman to provide security. I had to supply them with fuel. They even complained they did not have vehicles. So sometimes I would meet with them as the commander of the territory to help them deal with their problems, the problems they encountered in their work. Having said that, I would like to emphasize that they were not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. I'd like to turn your attention to a different area for a little while. And specifically, I want to take you back to a meeting you told the OTP about in 2004 during your interview. That meeting took place on the 2nd of September, 1992, in Bijeljina. Do you recall that meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that meeting? Please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was new to my duty as -- as a corps commander, and in the takeover of duties I received a document issued by the municipality of Bijeljina by which it ordered the command of the East Bosnia Corps to leave the territory not only of Bijeljina but entire Semberija and that the barracks should be handed over to a paramilitary formation called Tigrovi or also known as Arkan's Guard. I called the gentleman in question, whose name I can't remember at the moment - I believe that his name was Jokovic - and I told him that he did not have any authorities and that he cannot command the military and that what he sent me was sheer nonsense and it should be withdrawn. However, he was persistent, and he was impertinent, and he told me, First, obey the order and then complain. And then I took this document of his. I stapled it to my document, and I asked them to answer me, Who's my commander? Who is above me. And I sent that both to the Main Staff and also to the members of the presidency through the Main Staff, i.e., to the Supreme Command. I took that opportunity to talk to them as well. That same evening, General Mladic called me and asked me to meet him in the office, and he wanted to see the president as well -- the president was also supposed to come and that they would come with helicopter. However, two helicopters arrived later, but there was a general with his inner circle and present were the members of the presidency and some party members whom I didn't know that well. Then we all left to the municipality of Bijeljina, to whom he had sent an order before asking them for all the Assemblymen together. He wanted to see all the deputies and members of the Republika Srpska parliament, and I believe that a commissioner of the government for Semberija was also there, Mr. Miskin. In addition to the president, General Subotic was there as the Minister of Defence; I believe that the Minister of the Interior was also there; and prime minister, Mr. Dzeric. They were all there. After a very heated discussion that took place at the meeting, the president replaced the president of the municipality. I believe that he was taken into custody, and the other people who were present at the meeting also took part in the discussion. On the following day upon General Mladic's order, I briefed General Mladic and others with the situation in the corps, and I introduced them to my commanders who talked to him about the situation in their respective units. Well, that -- they did just to take the opportunity, since they were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General. I may not have asked my question clearly enough. Do you recall a meeting in which President Karadzic spoke and Mr. Krajisnik spoke, as well, and which was also attended by various corps commanders? We may be talking about the same meeting; we may not be, I just want to make sure we are before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we're talking about the same meeting. The objectives of the war, the strategic objectives of the war were put forth on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure. It's Friday, and I may be a little slow. Do you recall what President Karadzic spoke about at this meeting in addition to the topics you've already told us about? Just generally speaking, General.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after such a long time it's very difficult for me to remember, but I know that when we're talking about the strategic goals of the war, it wasn't him who put those forth. It was actually the speaker of the parliament, Mr. Krajisnik, who did that. President Karadzic spoke mostly about the local issues, the interference of the local government in the command of the military. He was rather angry, and he threatened the municipal authorities and his people from the party, warning them that this should not repeat again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And both General Mladic and General Gvero were there, and they both addressed this gathering, as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and the basic thesis that they supported at the meeting was the necessity to proclaim the state of war, which would lead to the normal functioning of every segment of society and put conditions in place for fighting in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I know that General Gvero said that the war had been opposed -- imposed upon us but that it was a just war - I remember that sentence very well - and that at all social capacities had to focus on that one task.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that Mr. Krajisnik spoke about the six strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was this the first time that you had heard of these strategic objectives, these six strategic objectives, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard those for the first time. I can repeat them. I don't know whether I can do it in the right order. The first goal was for us to be separated from the Muslims; the second goal was something to do with corridors, the corridor through Posavina and one to Herzegovina, I believe; the third was Sarajevo as a divided city; and the fourth, the border on the Drina, but the Serbian border on the Drina; the fifth was the border on the Neretva river; and the sixth goal was exit to the sea, if my memory serves me well. I believe it does. It was something more or less to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during your 2004 interview, you brought with you several notebooks or war diaries containing notes of meetings and so forth. The investigators copied your 1992 diary, but you made it clear that as for the rest of them, those contained your personal thoughts and private notes, and you preferred that they be kept secret, and we're going to respect that, General. But we do have your 1992 diary, so let's have a quick look at a couple of pages from that, and then I'll move on to some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3927 please, and if I have my math right, it will be page 35 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this, General, just so you know, if you see me looking away, I'm not being rude. I'm just making sure that I'm following the transcript, the simultaneous transcript. Now, if we look to the left at the bottom, you identify the speaker - and I'm sorry we don't have a translation of this in English. But --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, can you just read -- if you've identified who the speaker is, can you just tell us who that is there that you've underlined on the lower left at the bottom, there.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written in a hurry, and the handwriting is not really legible, but it was written by Mr. Krajisnik, and I can read you what I wrote if you want it to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, my question is actually more simple, and I'll just put it to you directly. Lower left-hand corner, you identify the speaker as the president of the assembly, Krajisnik; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. Now, if we look to the right, do you see where you've written "strategic goals"?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I haven't grown old yet. It's just the way I said it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just read what you wrote as you were listening to President -- Mr. Krajisnik present those objectives.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Strategic goals: "1. The first goal is separation from the Muslims. "2. Corridors. "3. Division of Sarajevo. "4. The Drina river valley - Serbs. "5. Border on the river Neretva. "6. Exit to the sea."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we're done with the General's notebook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, in your interview you referred to, and I quote: "The Serbian traditional aspiration of both sides of the Drina river." Can you just tell us as simply as you can, what does that mean when you told us about that in 2004 after reviewing these six strategic goals? Can you tell us how you understood that, what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ethnic area of the Serbs through the centuries stretched from Serbia through Bosnia-Herzegovina, partly Slavonia, and up to about half of Croatia. Unfortunately, because of wars and the large losses suffered by the Serbs in every war and especially in World War II, the ethnic map shrank little by little. However, among the people, the desire always persisted for the Serbs to live in a single state. This was achieved after World War II, but with the creation -- or, rather, with the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the creation of new states, this ceased to be the case, and the situation reverted to what it had been before World War I. The Bosnian Serbs always felt that Serbia was their homeland, their motherland, and their wish has always been to live in a single state with the Serbs in Serbia. This was especially strong, this feeling in the border areas between Bosnia and Serbia where the links - not only traffic links but also family links - were very well developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, during your interview, you made an observation in the context of the Srebrenica enclave and directive or -- I apologise, Strategic Goal 4. Is it fair to say that the -- with the Srebrenica enclave being situated where it is geographically, in the Drina river valley, that liberating Srebrenica was certainly key to achieving Strategic Goal number 4?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Drina river valley was Serbian even when the Srebrenica enclave was in existence, and it would probably not have been a problem at all had the enclave behaved as such, complying with international standards. It was a protected area, so it should have disarmed, and in that case, there would probably not have been any problems. There wouldn't have been any problems with the arrival of humanitarian aid, either. However, the units in the enclave remained armed. There were constant incursions against the surrounding Serbian villages, and this constantly worked to create a negative charge, not only among the surrounding population but all the inhabitants of the Republika Srpska and the wish to have Srebrenica finished once and for all, and probably the only way to do this was by military means. In my view, it would have been much better had it been done through negotiations or some sort of exchange of territories, but evidently the will for that did not exist on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, General, and you'll hear no argument from the Prosecution that the Bosnian Muslims in the Srebrenica enclave did some bad things, both before the establishment of the safe area and during its establishment. My question to you, though, is again, I think as you observed in your interview, with respect to the enclave itself and its position vis-a-vis that border that you were talking about, it was important to liberate that enclave in order to achieve that - as you said - traditional Serb dream of having a borderless Drina river valley?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat. Had the enclave been demilitarised and had it not represented a threat, no one would have interfered with it. I think that the decision of the political and military leaderships to defeat the enclave by military means was probably caused by the threat it posed. Whether it had anything to do with the goals of the war, well, as I've already said, from the source of the river --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, interpreter's correction: From the mouth of the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- apart from a small area in Zepa, the river Drina was in the hands of the Serbian army. I don't think that was the decisive factor. I may be wrong, Your Honours, but that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, I thought you provided you a very insightful encapsulation in your interview of how the strategic goals were translated into military tasks, and this was at page 138 of your interview. You said, and I quote: "So the armed forces, the army had to receive -- had to be given these strategic goals, which they were given, and then it was up to the Main Staff to transform this strategic goal, which is a political goal, into the military" -- and there is a word missing in the transcript, and maybe you can help us out with that -- "... through operations, through time planning, through use of manpower, forces, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the normal procedure, for politics to determine the goals. I have to say right away, it's politics that starts a war, wages a war, and ends a war. The military and the armed forces are only a means by which this is implemented. In wartime, it's implemented through the military. In peacetime, goals are implemented through political means. Strategic goals are put before the military, and the military has to implement short-term and long-term tasks. You have seen that one of the goals was the border on the Neretva, which we never achieved. One of the strategic goals was an exit to the sea, which we never had achieved. Even the division of Sarajevo was not done properly because we only a very small part of Sarajevo in these demarcations and so on. Whether this was the primary goal of politics, I don't know because it became topical because of events on the ground. Well, I can't say whether it did or not, but as a rule it's the politicians or, rather, the Supreme Commander, the Supreme Defence Counsel that sets the strategic goals and -- and imposes a time-frame on what has to be done. Let me repeat: It would have been much easier had a state of war been declared. I am convinced the war would not have lasted for four years, and it would have been waged according to all the principles that should be upheld in a just way and that all the crimes that unfortunately occurred would not have occurred. As a rule, or, rather, in general, I can answer your question as follows: It's politics that sets the goals and the military that implements them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you spoke - I think it was yesterday, General - about the annual process of analysis, learning from the prior year's successes and failures, and how that process leads to the Main Staff and the Supreme Command drafting the strategic tasks that are to be implemented in the forthcoming period. I just want to make sure I've got -- I've understood your testimony correctly. We saw the 1994 briefing on combat readiness being conducted at the very end of January of 1995, and then just over a month later, Directive 7 is issued. Do I have that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was it the case that directives would typically follow these combat readiness briefings?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, a directive is a general document, and it ought to reflect the tasks for at a year; but because of the situation on the ground and various new details that come up, it can be issued more frequently if some things cease to be valid or other things come up, and that's what happened in 1992, for example. We had three or four directives - or it may have been 1993; I don't remember anymore - and then there came a time when there was only one directive per year.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So to condense it just a bit, General, would you agree that Directive 7 is an example of what you've spoken about, what you've been speaking about, this transformation of the strategic political goals into concrete military tasks to achieve those goals?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. The commander of the Main Staff of the Supreme Commander can issue a directive. In this case, he was present at the briefing and he issued the directive, and it was only drawn up by persons in the Main Staff who did the technical part of the job. But it's a result of the consultation that was held, and it reflects the tasks set by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the case of Directive 7, that does go back to the briefing that was held at the end of January; is that fair to say, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the couple of minutes we've got left today, and on the topic of politicians, during the war you never joined the SDS, did you, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, or after the war either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there ever any attempt to get you to join, any influence brought on you to do that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Once, even the president of the republic came to see me and tried to persuade me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the JNA, you were a member of the Communist Party because the fact was you couldn't be an officer without being a member; is that fair to say, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a one-party system, and I said to the president, We are creating a new kind of society now with a multi-party system. I do not wish to be the general of a single party. I wish to be a general of the people, of the whole army, and for this reason I don't want to join any political party. I feel this is incompatible with the duty of an officer because then if the government changes, we have to change all the officers, and officers are experts. They're professionals. That wouldn't be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were a corps commander, for example, you faced hostility from local, municipal, political authorities because they didn't trust you; they called you an old communist, for example. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the members of the party who were in power mistrusted us because we did not join their party. That's why they paid more attention to the reserve officers than they did to us who are professional officers. Throughout the war, I felt that I was there due to force of circumstances, because of my professional knowledge, but if they had someone else that they would replace me very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And yourself and other professional JNA-trained officers were, in fact, branded as old communists or un -- reconstructed communists and so forth; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whoever held any responsible post in the former Yugoslavia could not do so unless he was a communist. We used to say that you couldn't even be the security man at the door or a fireman if he didn't join the communist party; and once the war broke out, only we officers were treated as old communists, and everybody else pretended they hadn't been communists. And when they had nothing else to hold against me, they would say, You're an old communist. Well, I had been, but I wasn't anymore. But the person saying that had also been a communist before, and he said, Well, I've renounced that. Had I not renounced it, I would not have participated in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, we are going to stop here. We'll continue Monday in the morning. In the meantime, have a nice weekend, and please refrain from communicating with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm disappointed. I am here for the 14th day now. I thought we would be finished before that. I thought I would be at home over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had hoped, too, but at least you will be able to enjoy the weather. Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid any confusion, I wanted to tell you that the following witness is not on the list for next week because we thought that he would be able to testify this week. It's the witness that's to be found on the list for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. So we stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
